scenes.tts: A pellet named mitochondria is never only mitochondria. So how do you find out what is really in it? In 1955 a group in Louvain broke rat liver gently, so the organelles stayed mostly whole, and spun it into five fractions. They measured enzymes in every fraction. The mitochondrial marker peaked in one place. Acid phosphatase did not travel with it.
scenes.visual: A pellet of mixed dots with a question mark; liver is spun into five tubes N M L P S; percent-of-activity bars for the two enzymes grow under the tubes and the peaks sit in different fractions.
scenes.narration: A pellet named mitochondria is never only mitochondria. So how do you find out what is really in it? In 1955 a group in Louvain broke rat liver gently, so the organelles stayed mostly whole, and spun it into five fractions. They measured enzymes in every fraction. scenes.tts: Here is a made-up table for rat liver. Each row adds up to one hundred percent. Take the percent of an enzyme found in a fraction, and divide by the percent of the protein found there. This is the relative specific activity. Fraction L holds forty-five percent of the acid phosphatase in five percent of the protein. Forty-five over five is nine. The fraction is enriched nine-fold.

scenes.visual: Zoom to fraction L: a short grey protein bar (5%) and a tall blue activity bar (45%); the tall bar is divided by the short one and becomes a bar of 9.0 against a baseline of 1.

scenes.tts: Now do the same for every fraction. Cytochrome oxidase, the mitochondrial marker, peaks in fraction M. Acid phosphatase, the lysosome marker, peaks in fraction L. An unknown enzyme, called X, follows acid phosphatase, fraction by fraction. It does not follow cytochrome oxidase.
scenes.visual: Grouped bars of relative specific activity over N M L P S build up one enzyme at a time: cytochrome oxidase peaks at M, acid phosphatase at L, and X's bars match acid phosphatase.
scenes.narration: Now do the same for every fraction. Cytochrome oxidase, the mitochondrial marker, peaks in fraction M. Acid phosphatase, the lysosome marker, peaks in fraction L. An unknown enzyme, called X, follows acid phosphatase, fraction by fraction. It does not follow cytochrome oxidase.

scenes.tts: But enriched does not mean pure. Fraction L also carries fifteen percent of the cell's cytochrome oxidase. For mitochondria, that is a relative specific activity of three in the same fraction. More than half the acid phosphatase is elsewhere. So L is enriched in lysosomes, but it is not pure. That is why several markers are read together.

scenes.visual: The three bars of fraction L are enlarged; the cytochrome oxidase bar is lit and labelled, and a tag says enriched, not pure.

scenes.tts: Next question. Is X inside a particle, or stuck to the outside of it? Latency is a test for this. It is activity that cannot be measured until a membrane is opened. Suppose only ten percent of the activity of X can be measured in intact particles. Add detergent, and it rises to one hundred percent. The substrate cannot reach an enzyme sealed behind a membrane. So X is ninety percent latent, and sits inside.

scenes.visual: A membrane-bound particle with X inside; substrate stays outside and a gauge reads 10; detergent opens the membrane, substrate enters, and the gauge rises to 100.

scenes.tts: So X is provisionally lysosomal. To confirm it, you want a second lysosomal marker that tracks X on a density gradient, and images of the protein in intact cells. A shared peak alone can come from two organelles that sediment together. Read the whole distribution, and never take a pellet's name for its contents.
scenes.visual: X gets a provisional lysosome tag; two checks are listed; two different organelles fall into one band, giving one shared peak.
